Apple has introduced its first-ever foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. The foldable iPhone Duo features a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer display, while the iPhone 18 Pro models bring a new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture and longer battery life. All three models run on the A20 Pro chip, while the iPhone Duo is eSIM-only.Apple has also announced India pricing, storage variants and availability for the new models. Here’s a detailed look at the prices, availability and key features of the newly launched iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models.The iPhone Duo comes in Star White and Night Sky colours. It is available in four storage options.Pre-orders for iPhone Duo begin October 16, with availability starting October 23 in India and more than 70 countries and regions. The phone will become available in another 28 countries and regions from October 30. iPhone Duo comes with an eSIM-only design worldwide. Apple says more than 500 carriers support eSIM, including Airtel, Jio and Vi.​The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max come in black, silver, glacier and burgundy finishes. Both models are available in four storage options.Pre-orders for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max begin September 12, with availability starting September 18 in India and more than 65 countries and regions.The two models will become available in another 20 countries and regions from September 25.Both models come with iOS 27 and support Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. eSIM-only models are available in select markets, while India is among the countries included in the initial launch.Apple's iPhone Duo, the company's first foldable iPhone, opens to a 7.6-inch display, which is the largest ever on an iPhone. It folds down to a 5.4-inch outer Super Retina XDR screen that Apple says offers 90 per cent of the screen area of the iPhone 18 Pro. Both displays share the same aspect ratio for proportional scaling, support ProMotion, Always-On functionality and up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness, and the inner display uses a nano-texture, glare-reducing finish with an under-display FaceTime camera.The device is built from grade 5 titanium with a mirror-polished finish, Ceramic Shield on the back and the tougher Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, and carries an IP68 water/dust resistance rating. Its hinge has over 100 components, reinforced with support ribs and ceramic fibre inserts for added rigidity.iPhone Duo has a 48MP Fusion Main camera, a 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide (shared with the iPhone 18 Pro), and a Center Stage front camera. Fold-specific features include Smart Take, Duo Preview, Kid Cue and Duo FaceTime, plus 4K/120fps Dolby Vision video recording.It ships with iOS 27, redesigned for the foldable form factor with side-mounted controls, dual Home Screen pages, Split View multitasking, an upgraded StandBy mode, and a beta rollout of Siri AI, which can use personal context and on-screen content to answer questions or take actions.The phone runs on Apple’s 2nm A20 Pro chip (6-core CPU, 7-core GPU, dual 16-core Neural Engine) with a vapour chamber cooling system. Dual batteries can last up to 31 hours of video on the inner display, 44 hours on the outer display or 24 hours of mixed use, and it has fast wired and wireless charging.It uses Apple's N1 chip (Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread) and the C2 modem for improved cellular performance, with Apple Pencil (USB-C) support planned later this year.Display: Both models feature Super Retina XDR displays with ProMotion, Always-On functionality and up to 3,000 nits of peak outdoor brightness. The Dynamic Island has been redesigned to take up less space while showing more information, including up to three Live Activities at once.The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feature a new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture, bringing manual aperture control to the iPhone for the first time. The six-blade system offers four aperture settings and can automatically adjust based on lighting and depth of field. These phones also get upgraded Photographic Styles, Pro controls for settings such as shutter speed and white balance, and a histogram for checking exposure. Apple Reference Image can create a reference version of a photo using signed sensor data to help determine whether an image has been edited. Video features include Cinematic effects after capture at up to 60fps, 4K Dolby Vision HDR time-lapse and an updated Audio Mix.Both models are powered by Apple's 2nm A20 Pro chip with a 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. Apple says the GPU is up to 40 per cent faster than the A19 Pro, while the Neural Engine delivers twice the AI processing power. The phones also use a redesigned vapour chamber with three times more surface area than the previous generation, enabling up to 40 per cent higher sustained performance, according to Apple.The iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback on eSIM-only models, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers up to 45 hours. The iPhone 18 Pro can charge up to 50 per cent in around 15 minutes and wirelessly charge up to 50 per cent in 30 minutes. Apple says five minutes of wired charging on the iPhone 18 Pro Max provides around seven hours of video playback, while the phone can offer up to 30 hours of usage on a full charge based on its new battery usage model.Both phones ship with iOS 27 and support Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. Siri AI can use personal context from messages, emails and photos, understand onscreen content and help users find information or perform actions. iOS 27 also introduces iPhone Handoff, allowing users with supported carriers to switch between two iPhone models using the same phone number.The iPhone 18 Pro models feature Apple's N1 wireless chip with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. They also introduce the C2 cellular modem system, which Apple says provides faster uploads than C1X while consuming 15 per cent less energy.
Article Summary: Apple has introduced its first-ever foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. The foldable phone features a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer display. iPhone 18 Pro models bring a new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture. All three models run on the A20 Pro chip, while iPhone Duo is eSIM-only.

Article Text:

Apple has launched its next-generation Apple Watch series — Apple Watch Series 12 at the company’s ‘Surprise and Shine ’ event on September 9. With a starting price tag of Rs 56,900, the Apple Watch Series 12 promises to offer most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable, higher-frequency heart rate and HRV sensing along with the Audio Intelligence features. We spent some time with the Apple Watch Series 12, and here are our initial impressions of Apple’s latest wearable.At first glance, Series 12 sticks close to the design language Apple Watch has settled into over the past several generations, and that's a deliberate choice rather than a lack of ambition. It comes in the now-familiar 42mm and 46mm sizes, with aluminium models refreshed in dark bronze, black, light gold, and the returning space gray, alongside titanium options in a new radiant gold finish and the existing natural titanium. A striking ceramic version rounds out the lineup in pearl white and night blue, complete with a ceramic pin-and-tuck closure on its matching Sport Bands that pairs nicely with the case.The more meaningful design change is durability rather than aesthetics: aluminum models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60% tougher than the Ion-X glass on the previous generation. In practice, that's the kind of upgrade you don't notice until the first accidental knock against a doorframe, but it's a welcome move given how often a watch takes small hits over the course of a day.The overall build still feels thin and light on the wrist, in keeping with Apple's continued push to make the watch comfortable enough to wear overnight for sleep tracking without it feeling bulky.Apple hasn't dramatically reworked the display itself this generation, and that's mostly fine. the existing Retina display across aluminum, titanium, and ceramic cases remains sharp, bright, and easy to read at a glance, now protected by the tougher Ceramic Shield 2 cover on aluminum models. Where the display does feel genuinely new is in what it's showing: a new heart rate watch face complication puts real-time heart rate front and center, updating far more frequently than before thanks to the watch's upgraded sensors, and a new Steps complication does the same for step count, both readable in a quick glance without opening an app.The Smart Stack also gets more capable this round, with new contextual widget suggestions — like a parked-car reminder or a birthday nudge for a close contact — surfacing right on the display exactly when they're relevant, alongside a new single-handed tap gesture for selecting individual widgets without needing a second hand free.This is where Series 12 makes its real case for an upgrade. At the center of it all is Apple's new Health Sensing System, paired with the S11 chip, which Apple says delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing of any wearable currently on the market — a claim backed by a study spanning more than 1,000 participants comparing it against competing devices.In daily use, the difference shows up in frequency as much as accuracy: the watch now measures heart rate every five seconds throughout the day, a dramatic jump from previous generations, and tracks heart rate variability up to 24 times more often, split into two distinct metrics — recovery HRV for day-to-day stress signals, and overall HRV for a broader read on cardiovascular health.That denser stream of data feeds directly into the watch's headline new feature: readiness. Each day, Series 12 combines recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score into a single 0-10 score, paired with a plain-language recommendation — Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. It's a small addition on paper, but in use it functions as a genuinely useful daily gut-check, updating in real time if, say, an intense workout or a shift in vitals changes the picture partway through the day.Battery life sees a solid, if incremental, bump — up to 10 hours during an outdoor workout, a 25% improvement over the previous model, alongside faster charging that now delivers up to 12 hours of extra battery from just 15 minutes on the charger. Step tracking has also been quietly overhauled with new machine learning models, and Apple now claims it as the most accurate step tracking of any smartwatch on the market. Another important additions this time are the new Audio Intelligence features which are said to arrive later this tear. The Live Rewind feature enables you to double-press the Digital Crown and instantly the last b15 seconds of a conversation as text. This is a clever new way to catchup with something you half-missed without asking the other person to repeat. Another interesting feature is Siri Recap which goes further and generate a title and key points from a conversation afterward so that you can revisit it later. Also, Sound Recognition extends existing accessibility features to the wrist, alerting users who are deaf or hard of hearing to sounds like doorbells, alarms, or a crying baby even without an iPhone nearby. Apple has clearly built privacy into the foundation of these features rather than bolting it on afterward — audio is processed in an isolated hardware compartment on the S11 chip and immediately discarded, nothing is stored as a recording, and features like Live Rewind visibly and audibly signal to people nearby when they're active.Layered on top of all this is Siri AI, arriving with watchOS 27, which brings genuine personal context awareness and broader conversational ability to the wrist for the first time, accessible through a new Siri Modular watch face.Apple Watch Series 12 isn't trying to reinvent what a smartwatch looks like, and that's precisely why it works. The real story here is underneath the display: a genuinely more capable set of health sensors, a readiness score that turns raw vitals into something immediately actionable, and Audio Intelligence features that feel thoughtfully built around privacy. None of it demands you change how you use your watch day to day, but all of it makes the data you're already generating meaningfully more useful. With a starting price of Rs 56,900, the Apple Watch Series 12 offers a compelling upgrade to users coming from Series 8 or earlier.
Article Summary: Apple has launched its next-generation Apple Watch series. Apple Watch Series 12 was unveiled at the company’s ‘Surprise and Shine ’ event on September 9. With a starting price tag of Rs 56,900, it promises to offer most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable, higher-frequency heart rate and HRV sensing.

Article Text:

Apple Watch Ultra 4 doesn't change what the Ultra line looks like on your wrist, but it changes what it knows about you while it's there. Apple has refreshed its Watch Ultra lineup with the launch of all new Apple Watch Ultra 4 at the company’s ’Surprise Shine’ event on September 9. Successor to the Apple Watch Ultra 3, the Ultra 4 feature new Health Sensing System, which claims to provide the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable, powerful insights including readiness and longer battery life. We had the chance to spend some time with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and here are our initial impressions of Apple’s latest rugged wearable.Apple Watch Ultra 4 keeps the rugged, unmistakable Ultra silhouette, available in the same natural and black titanium finishes as before. It's a design Apple has clearly settled on as the right one for its most durable watch, and there's no attempt to reinvent it here — the case still feels substantial on the wrist without tipping into cumbersome, and the titanium build continues to feel like it's genuinely built for the outdoors rather than just styled to look like it.The band lineup gets a proper refresh this year. Trail Loop adds dark umber, sand, and burgundy options, while Alpine Loop picks up desert, dark olive, and burgundy.The most interesting material change is on the Ocean Band, now made from a unique translucent silicone available in translucent gray, translucent kelp, and translucent black — a genuinely different look from the solid-colour bands Apple has offered in the past, and one that feels distinctly suited to the Ultra's adventure-sport identity. For Hermès buyers, the collection adds a striking new Grand H titanium band with a built-in extension mechanism that lets it stretch to fit over a wet suit — a small but thoughtful detail for anyone actually using the watch the way Apple markets it.Apple didn't make display technology the headline story with Ultra 4, and that continues a trend from recent Ultra generations — the large, bright, titanium-wrapped display that's made the Ultra legible in direct sunlight and usable with gloves on remains the foundation here. Where the display does become more useful this year is through software: a new heart rate watch face complication surfaces real-time heart rate data at a glance, and a new Steps complication does the same for step count, both readable instantly without opening a separate app. The Smart Stack also becomes more capable, with contextual suggestions — like a parked-car reminder from Maps — surfacing directly on screen, plus a new single-handed tap gesture for selecting individual widgets without needing a free hand.This is where Apple Watch Ultra 4 makes its real case for an upgrade. At the core is Apple's new Health Sensing System paired with the S11 chip, which Apple says delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing of any wearable currently available — validated in a study spanning more than 1,000 participants against competing devices. In daily use, the most noticeable change is frequency: heart rate is now measured every five seconds, all day long, and heart rate variability is tracked up to 24 times more often than before, split into recovery HRV for day-to-day stress signals and overall HRV for broader cardiovascular insight.That denser data stream feeds directly into readiness, the watch's headline new feature. Each day, Ultra 4 combines recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score into a single 0-10 score paired with a clear recommendation — Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It — and it updates in real time as new data comes in, whether that's from an intense workout or a shift in daytime vitals. For an audience of athletes and endurance competitors, having that kind of daily gut-check feels like a genuinely practical addition rather than just another number to track.Battery life sees a substantial jump. Everyday use now stretches to up to 50 hours, and Low Power Mode extends that to as much as 84 hours — genuinely multi-day territory for a device this capable. Charging is also faster, with just 15 minutes on the charger adding up to 18 hours of battery back. For outdoor athletes specifically, the new Extended Workout mode delivers up to 25 hours of tracking with full GPS and heart rate data, a 25% jump over the previous model, while the new Max Extended Workout mode stretches that to 45 hours — enough, Apple notes, to track a full 100-mile race while still logging GPS readings every second. Step tracking has also been overhauled with new machine learning models, and Apple now claims it as the most accurate step tracking of any smartwatch, alongside claiming the most accurate on-device GPS in a sports watch.The most forward-looking additions are the new Audio Intelligence features arriving later this year. Live Rewind lets you double-press the Digital Crown to instantly pull up the last 15 seconds of a conversation as text — genuinely useful mid-run or mid-hike when you half-catch something a training partner said. Siri Recap goes further, generating a title and key points from a conversation afterward for later review, and Sound Recognition extends accessibility features to the wrist, alerting users who are deaf or hard of hearing to sounds like sirens or alarms even without an iPhone nearby. Apple has clearly built privacy into these features from the ground up rather than adding it as an afterthought: audio is processed in an isolated hardware compartment on the S11 chip and immediately discarded, nothing is stored as a recording, and features like Live Rewind visibly and audibly signal to people nearby when they're active.Layered on top is Siri AI, arriving with watchOS 27, bringing genuine personal context awareness to the wrist, accessible through a new Siri Modular watch face — a meaningful step up from Siri's previous, more limited capabilities on Apple Watch.Apple Watch Ultra 4 doesn't ask you to fall in love with a new shape or a flashier screen — it asks you to trust that its sensors, battery, and software have all gotten meaningfully smarter since last year, and on that front, it delivers. The jump to five-second heart rate sensing, the introduction of readiness as an actual daily decision-making tool, and battery life stretching to 45 hours of full GPS tracking for ultra-endurance events are all substantial, practical improvements for the athletes and adventurers this watch is built for. For the complete analysis on the Watch Ultra 4 you will have to wait for our detailed review.
Article Summary: Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the successor to the Apple Watch Ultra 3. New Health Sensing System claims to provide the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable. New Extended Workout mode delivers up to 25 hours of tracking with full GPS and heart rate data.

Article Title: How Apple iPhone Duo got Samsung and Google in an 'ugly fight'
Article Text:
Apple iPhone Duo got Samsung and Google in an 'ugly fight'

Samsung says Apple ‘copied us too’

Duolingo responds to Samsung

Samsung and Apple have a long-running rivalry

Apple’s launch of its first foldable phone, iPhone Duo has triggered a social media exchange between Samsung and Duolingo after Samsung compared Apple’s new foldable phone with its own foldable devices. What started as Samsung’s joke about Apple copying its technology quickly turned into a separate exchange with Duolingo, with the two brands trading posts over the iPhone Duo’s name and design. The posts have drawn millions of views on X, turning the iPhone Duo launch into another round of social media rivalry between major technology brands.Samsung Mobile US started sharing comments shortly after Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo. The Samsung Mobile US account posted on X (formerly Twitter):“I'm so sorry, @duolingo. They copied us too #Solidarity”The post was aimed at Duolingo because Apple’s new foldable phone uses the name Duo. Samsung was also referring to the foldable design, an area where the company has released Galaxy Z-series phones for several years.Duolingo quickly joined the exchange. The language-learning platform responded to Samsung:“when an ugly stranger calls you twin No Brand”Samsung then replied directly: “Ugly?? Watch your language...”Duolingo continued the joke, writing:“sorry twin heat of the moment twin.. please don’t break my app on your phones twin”The exchange turned the Samsung vs Duolingo interaction into a separate viral moment around Apple’s iPhone Duo launch.Samsung and Apple have competed in the smartphone market for years, with both companies regularly using advertising and social media to target each other.Samsung has previously criticised Apple for adopting features that were already available on Galaxy phones. Apple, meanwhile, has continued to expand the iPhone lineup into new categories.Samsung later posted another message aimed at Apple: “Let us know when you're done reheating our leftovers”“Not the bed side clock. It's giving groundhog day,” the company shared in another post. “Making us wait? Fine. We'll be over here, folding 3 ways,” reads another post.The comments were part of Samsung’s wider reaction to Apple’s iPhone launch on X.
Article Summary: Samsung compared Apple’s new foldable phone with its own foldable devices. What started as a joke about Apple copying its technology quickly turned into a separate exchange with Duolingo. The posts have drawn millions of views on X, turning the iPhone Duo launch into another round of social media rivalry.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: In Gateshead, water trapped 150 metres below the city in abandoned coal mines now heats 350 homes and public buildings
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Mine water heat pump powers Gateshead buildings

Why does mine water get warmer with depth

Image AI generated

What is the Gateshead living laboratory studying

Water trapped deep beneath Gateshead is now helping heat hundreds of homes and public buildings, turning former coal mine workings into a source of heat for the city. The water lies around 150 metres below Gateshead town centre, where a 6-megawatt water-source heat pump extracts its heat and feeds it into an existing district heating network. According to the Mining Remediation Authority, the system went live on 29 March 2023 after about three years of work and is the largest mine water heat network in Great Britain. More than 5 kilometres of heat-network pipes carry the heat to buildings including Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, several offices and 350 council-owned homes. The network is also planned to reach another 270 privately owned homes, alongside a new conference centre and hotel development. The project is also being studied through the Gateshead Living Laboratory, where boreholes and monitoring equipment collect data on the mine water system.A 6 megawatt water-source heat pump recovers heat from the mine water and transfers it into the district heating network. The heated water is then distributed through more than 5 kilometres of heat-network pipes to connected buildings.The network currently supplies heat to several types of buildings across Gateshead.These include Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, several offices and 350 council-owned homes. The source states that the system is also planned to serve another 270 privately owned homes, as well as a new conference centre and a hotel development.Mine water becomes warmer with increasing depth because of what the Mining Remediation Authority describes as a ‘geothermal gradient’. Mine water temperatures generally range from 10°C to 20°C, although they can reach 40°C at depths of around 1 kilometre. Water can be brought to the surface through boreholes, shafts or adits, before heat exchangers and pumps recover its heat. The authority says mine water temperatures are not affected by seasonal variations. It describes mine water as a potential source of “renewable, secure, low carbon heating for buildings in coalfield areas”, with the right support and sustainable management.The Gateshead mine water heating network is part of a wider research project known as the Gateshead Living Laboratory. The initiative is designed to collect evidence that supports future licensing, management and wider use of mine water heat schemes. It is located near three mine water heat schemes in the North East of England.With support from Gateshead Council, researchers drilled four boreholes and installed monitoring equipment to gather data. The information is available as open-access data for researchers, regulators, stakeholders and academic institutions. The government says the work will help researchers study the thermal and hydrogeological interactions between multiple mine water heat schemes in the Walker mining block in Tyne and Wear.
Article Summary: A 6 megawatt water-source heat pump recovers heat from the mine water and transfers it into the district heating network. The heated water is then distributed through more than 5 kilometres of heat-network pipes to connected buildings. The network currently supplies heat to several types of buildings across Gateshead. These include Gateshead College, the Baltic Arts Centre, several offices and 350 council-owned homes.

Article Title: Spanish cave remains reveal repeated cannibalism in prehistoric Europe, from violent deaths to human skulls turned into cups
Article Text:
Image: Cut marks on adult human skull from Majolicas Cave/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Ancient Spanish caves preserve evidence of repeated cannibalism

Cannibalism appeared during several distinct prehistoric periods

Some remains reveal possible episodes of prehistoric violence

Human skulls were transformed into objects after death

Ancient human remains from three caves in southern Spain are revealing a disturbing but complex chapter in Europe’s prehistoric past. Researchers examined nearly 1,000 human bones from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela and Majolicas caves in Granada, finding evidence that people cut, fractured, chewed and deliberately modified human remains during different periods of the Neolithic. The findings suggest cannibalism was not one continuous tradition, but a practice that appeared repeatedly in different contexts over thousands of years, offering clues about prehistoric violence, death and ritual.The remains come from three caves in Granada that have provided archaeologists with evidence of prehistoric human activity for decades. Researchers in ' Multiphase human cannibalism in Neolithic southern Iberia: Chronological and taphonomic evidence from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela, and Majolicas Caves ,' published in Journal of Archaeological Science examined the bones for microscopic traces including cut marks, fractures, impact damage and tooth marks, while also studying how and when the damage occurred. Their analysis found evidence consistent with deliberate processing of human remains at all three sites, although the circumstances varied considerably. At Malalmuerzo, some remains appear connected with violent deaths, while Carigüela contained deliberately modified human skulls. At Majolicas, the treatment of human remains appears to have had a different cultural context, showing that the discovery cannot be reduced to one explanation for prehistoric cannibalism.Rather than suggesting that Neolithic Europeans regularly consumed human flesh, the evidence indicates several separate episodes spread across thousands of years. The researchers identified concentrations around the end of the sixth millennium BC, the middle of the fifth millennium BC and the end of the third millennium BC. At Carigüela, evidence indicates several episodes of cannibalism during the Neolithic, including the deliberate modification of two human skulls into cup-like objects. At Majolicas, the most recent evidence dates to approximately 3800 BC. The pattern suggests that cannibalism repeatedly emerged under particular circumstances rather than representing a permanent or universal feature of prehistoric communities.One of the most striking sets of evidence comes from Malalmuerzo, where fractures and other damage to the bones indicate that some individuals may have died violently. The remains belonged to people of different ages, leading researchers to consider whether a group could have been attacked, killed and subsequently consumed. This interpretation potentially connects cannibalism with conflict between prehistoric communities. However, the researchers do not treat every damaged bone as proof of warfare. The contrasting evidence from the three caves demonstrates that human remains could be processed in different ways and for different reasons, including possible conflict, consumption and cultural or ritual practices.The discoveries at Carigüela offer some of the clearest evidence that the treatment of human remains was not necessarily motivated by hunger alone. Two skulls were deliberately modified into cups, suggesting that parts of the human body could acquire a new symbolic or practical purpose after death. The researchers therefore argue against viewing “Neolithic cannibalism” as one uniform practice. Similar marks on human bones can emerge from very different circumstances, and the archaeological record points towards a complicated relationship between death, the body and community life. These recurring episodes provide a rare glimpse into how prehistoric societies dealt with violence, the dead and relationships between groups.
Article Summary: Researchers examined nearly 1,000 human bones from Malalmuerzo, Carigüela and Majolicas caves in Granada. They found evidence that people cut, fractured, chewed and deliberately modified human remains during different periods of the Neolithic. The findings suggest cannibalism was not one continuous tradition, but a practice that appeared repeatedly over thousands of years.

Article Title: Spain released wild horses into the Iberian Highlands after a 10,000-year absence; the animals are being used to rebuild a fire-prone landscape
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Spain’s wild horses rebuild a fire-prone landscape

Wild horses create a natural firebreak

Image AI generated

Wild horses expand large-herbivore grazing in Spain

Przewalski’s horses are roaming Spain’s Iberian Highlands again after an absence of more than 10,000 years, as a rewilding project uses the animals’ natural grazing to reshape a landscape increasingly vulnerable to wildfires. The horses were released in Villanueva de Alcorón, Guadalajara province, as part of an effort by Rewilding Spain to restore the ecological role once played by large wild herbivores. Their grazing and trampling reduce vegetation and forest biomass, while helping create a more varied landscape of woodland and open pasture. The return of the horses follows their near-extinction in the 20th century and represents a new stage in efforts to restore natural processes across the Iberian Highlands. According to Rewilding Spain, an environmental conservation initiative, the animals can help improve pasture quality and support biodiversity, while reducing the amount of combustible vegetation. The project is an opportunity for visitors to observe horses living freely in Western Europe.The horses are not being released simply to increase the number of wild animals in the region. Their grazing is intended to replace an ecological function that was lost after extensive livestock farming, with horses and cattle disappearing from parts of the Alto Tajo.As the animals feed and move through the landscape, they reduce vegetation and forest biomass while creating more varied pasture conditions.Rewilding Spain says natural grazing by large herbivores is important for restoring healthy ecosystems because feeding and trampling can reduce the amount of forest biomass available. The organisation states that the horses “reduce forest biomass available in the area”, while their grazing also improves the diversity and quality of pastures used by deer, roe deer, fallow deer and domestic sheep and goats.The Iberian Highlands have extensive areas of forest and vegetation where a lack of large grazers can allow shrubs and other plants to become denser. Rewilding Spain is using natural grazing as one way of changing that vegetation structure. By eating grasses, shrubs and other plants and moving through the landscape, the horses help create more open areas and a mixture of different vegetation types.The wider rewilding initiative explicitly links this work with wildfire prevention. Horses can help make landscapes more heterogeneous and richer in terms of biodiversity, which it considers important for reducing vulnerability to wildfires. Its Iberian Highlands programme also says horses are helping to open up areas affected by past fires, increasing structural diversity and creating a landscape mosaic that can support regeneration.The return of Przewalski’s horses is also part of a wider programme to restore large-herbivore grazing across the Iberian Highlands. Rewilding Spain is working with Przewalski’s horses alongside Serrano and Pottoka horses and tauros cattle in different parts of the landscape. The organisation says the combined management of large herbivores now covers tens of thousands of hectares, to support forest regeneration, biodiversity and wildfire prevention.The horses are also becoming part of the region’s nature-tourism economy. Their presence has already attracted visitors to Villanueva de Alcorón, where guided trips allow people to see the animals living independently in the landscape.
Article Summary: The horses were released in Villanueva de Alcorón, Guadalajara province, as part of an effort by Rewilding Spain to restore the ecological role once played by large wild herbivores. Their grazing and trampling reduce vegetation and forest biomass, while helping create a more varied landscape.

Article Title: Denmark planted trees for carbon storage, but 21 years later natural forests proved more diverse while plantations captured carbon faster
Article Text:
Image: Canva

What did scientists discover in Denmark after 21 years

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster?

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster? (Image: Canva)

Why were naturally regenerated forests more diverse?

What does the research mean for future forest restoration?

Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. After 21 years, scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures. The University of Copenhagen conducted a rare long-term comparison of two approaches to forest restoration and found why future reforestation projects may need to balance rapid carbon capture with biodiversity recovery and ecological complexity.The study ‘ Passive versus active afforestation of agricultural land: Two decades of impacts on tree biomass and ecosystem carbon storage ’ compared agricultural land that had been abandoned and allowed to regenerate naturally with areas that had been actively planted to create plantation forests. After approximately 21 years, clear differences had emerged between the two approaches. Plantation forests had accumulated substantially more tree biomass than naturally colonised forests, demonstrating that deliberate planting can accelerate early forest development and carbon storage.Naturally regenerated areas, however, developed a different ecological character as vegetation colonised the abandoned farmland without the same intensive planting approach. The researchers also compared these younger forests with mature, actively managed forests, providing a longer-term reference point. The findings show that forest recovery cannot be judged by carbon storage alone.The plantations had the advantage of being able to accumulate more biomass early in their life due to trees being purposefully planted instead of waiting for them to come naturally as part of the process of succession. This study shows that the plantation forests have 16 times more above-ground woody biomass compared to the naturally colonised forests within a period of about twenty years. As such, the faster accumulation of biomass led to faster accumulation of carbon in the trees within the early stage of forest development. It is important to note that fast biomass accumulation does not necessarily mean that the plantation mimics all the ecological features of a mature forest.The colonisation that occurred naturally enabled vegetation to grow by the means of ecological succession without any predetermined planting. This process will take more time, but will lead to greater diversity of plants in terms of their species and structure since different plants will colonise certain areas. The Danish study showed that the naturally colonised forests were distinct from the plantation in terms of vegetation and ecology, which proves the necessity of using natural factors in the process of creation of the forest. However, this statement does not mean that plantations cannot be valuable in terms of biodiversity, but only that the structure and composition of such forests differ greatly from the forests developed without planting.The results imply that there is no one particular forest restoration approach that would optimise all of the environmental benefits at once. Plantations would be an advantageous choice if the aim is to achieve rapid carbon sequestration because plantations would help to achieve faster carbon accumulation. As for natural regeneration, it would provide greater ecological diversity as the forest develops and could contribute significantly to biodiversity. Therefore, the scientists show a more complex view of afforestation that does not include only the number of trees planted.
Article Summary: Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. Scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures.

Article Title: Copenhagen’s £200m underground Natural History Museum, under construction since 2019, to open in 2027 with eight galleries, 14m specimens, dinosaur skeletons, 3D exhibits and Ocean Hall
Article Text:
Copenhagen’s £200 million Natural History Museum will open its new underground galleries in 2027. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

Eight galleries will be built underground

The new museum will feature eight immersive exhibitions covering the history of the natural world. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

The museum’s collection includes around 14 million specimens gathered over 400 years. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

14 million specimens include dinosaur skeletons

Interactive 3D exhibits will allow visitors to explore detailed digital scans of specimens. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

Ocean Hall features a huge glass dome

The spectacular Ocean Hall will feature a huge dome made with 1,600 triangular glass panels. (Photo: Natural History Museum Denmark)

£200 million project has taken years to complete

Museum will sit alongside Copenhagen’s Botanical Garden

A huge new underground attraction is set to open in one of Europe’s most popular cities, promising visitors immersive experiences, dinosaur fossils and access to millions of specimens collected over centuries.The new Natural History Museum in Copenhagen, Denmark, will officially open on March 6, 2027, following a major £200 million redevelopment project that has been years in the making.The centrepiece of the project is a series of eight new galleries built underground, creating a vast new exhibition space beneath Copenhagen’s historic Botanical Garden.The eight exhibitions will be titled Universe, Earth, Life, Denmark, Arctic, Biodiversity, Humans and Ocean Hall, taking visitors on a journey through the history of the natural world, according to The Official Copenhagen City Card website.The museum has been designed to combine Copenhagen’s historic architecture with a striking new underground complex.According to architect Lene Tranberg, natural light will reach the underground exhibition galleries through skylights, while the design aims to “engage all the senses”.Inside, visitors will find concrete interiors, curved staircases and large exhibition spaces designed to create an immersive journey through natural history.The new museum connects the Botanical Garden, the existing historic buildings and new architecture inspired by organic forms found in nature.The museum says the project represents a new direction in Danish museum architecture, combining protected historic surroundings with new underground galleries and above-ground structures inspired by nature.The museum is home to an extraordinary collection of around 14 million items gathered over 400 years, including fossils and specimens documenting the history and diversity of life on Earth.Among the highlights are dinosaur remains, including a 17-metre-long Diplodocus skeleton and T-Rex skeletons.Visitors will also be able to explore specimens using interactive touchscreen tables, allowing them to rotate and zoom into 3D scans of objects from the museum's collections.The exhibitions will cover everything from the formation of the Solar System and the origins of species to biodiversity and the rapidly changing natural world.The scale of the new museum can be seen in the construction details.The exhibition halls have walls reaching up to 10 metres high, while ceilings are made using around 180,000 small wooden slats, designed to improve acoustics across the large spaces.The Ocean Hall measures 16 metres wide, 23 metres high and 50 metres long. Its dome consists of 2,000 steel frames fitted with 1,600 triangular glass panels.Remarkably, only two of the glass panes in the entire structure are identical.The museum's welcome hall is housed in a former engine house that was dismantled and reconstructed using original facade bricks and steel lattice structures.The excavation for the foundations reached 15 metres deep and stretched 400 metres in circumference.Plans for the new museum were first revealed around 17 years ago, while construction began in 2019.The project was originally expected to open much earlier, but planning permission and funding issues contributed to significant delays.The exhibition concept was developed by the museum in collaboration with design agency Tinker Imagineers, which won an international competition in 2018. In 2023, the project entered its production phase, with Event Communications winning the contract to deliver the new permanent exhibitions.Christine Wiberg-Lyng, Foundation Director at Aage og Johanne Louis-Hansens Fond, said the new buildings create a sensory setting that supports the museum's core purpose.The redevelopment will add around 7,000 square metres of exhibition space, while another 2,000 square metres will include public facilities such as the shop, ticket office, VILLUM Hall, restaurant, café and dining areas.Around 500 square metres will be dedicated to teaching facilities for school students.Collection storage, laboratories, offices and other staff facilities will occupy approximately 22,500 square metres. Overall, the new museum will comprise around 32,000 square metres, divided almost equally between new construction and renovated historic buildings.Above the underground galleries, Copenhagen's Botanical Garden offers visitors a living museum containing around 13,000 plant species, alongside alpine rock gardens and walking trails.The site also includes the Palm House and Butterfly House, located inside a Victorian cast-iron glasshouse dating back to 1874.The Botanical Garden is free to enter, while tickets for the new museum are listed at approximately £13.22 for adults and £5.75 for children aged three to 17.
Article Summary: Copenhagen’s £200 million Natural History Museum will open its new underground galleries in 2027. The new museum will feature eight immersive exhibitions covering the history of the natural world. The museum is home to an extraordinary collection of around 14 million items gathered over 400 years, including dinosaur remains.

Article Title: In 1978, Massachusetts dumped concrete-filled tyres into the ocean; decades later, they had become a thriving habitat for marine life
Article Text:
Massachusetts built its first permitted artificial reef with concrete-filled tyres

The underwater structures showed little sign of drifting away

The 2019 survey revealed how quickly fish found the reef

The tyre bundles created shelter and surfaces for marine life

New structures continued to reshape the Yarmouth reef

A pile of concrete-filled tyres may not look like much from above, but beneath the surface it can become something very different. Off Yarmouth, Massachusetts, the unusual structures form part of an artificial reef that has been developing in Nantucket Sound since 1978. The project was designed to introduce physical complexity to a sandy seabed and provide habitat for fish and lobsters. Over time, the reef expanded to roughly 2,500 original units across 127 acres, while later additions brought in concrete and granite. Surveys in 2019 gave researchers another way to measure its effect, revealing a striking difference in how quickly fish reached structured reef habitat and bare sand.The Yarmouth reef was developed by the town's Department of Natural Resources with assistance from the Division of Marine Fisheries. It became the first permitted artificial reef of its kind in Massachusetts and was positioned more than two miles south of the mouth of Bass River.The original units were relatively simple. Three to five tyres were filled with concrete and fastened together in bundles, creating a low structure above the seabed.About 1,500 units went into the water in 1978, followed by another 1,000 in 1994, bringing the total to roughly 2,500. The aim was to introduce physical complexity into an otherwise relatively featureless stretch of bottom, giving fish and lobsters places to shelter and move around.Massachusetts' artificial reef programme describes such structures as deliberately placed habitat for fish, with potential benefits for fisheries and recreational fishing.Surveys conducted by the Division of Marine Fisheries in 2009 and 2010 used side-scan sonar and divers to examine the site. They found little evidence of reef material moving outside the permitted area. The northern part of the site contained the highest concentration of deployed material, while fish numbers were also higher where more reef structure was present. Scup and black sea bass were among the fish found in substantial numbers.The structures were being managed as habitat. The Massachusetts artificial reef programme uses surveys, diving and remote sensing to track how these sites perform and how marine communities develop around them.In a 2019 survey, researchers compared the Yarmouth reef with another artificial reef, a natural reef and an area of relatively featureless bottom. Underwater video cameras were used to observe fish arriving at the different sites.The contrast was striking in terms of arrival time, without needing a dramatic interpretation. Finfish appeared on camera after an average of about 33 seconds at reef sites, compared with 502 seconds at the bare control. That is roughly eight minutes and 22 seconds over the unstructured seabed. The study calculated that fish appeared on reef sites 93.4% faster than at the bare control.The result did not mean every reef was identical. The study also measured species richness and diversity at Yarmouth, Harwich, a natural reef and the bare control. Black sea bass and scup were among the species recorded across the sites, while the researchers found differences in the composition of fish communities depending on the location and reef age.The value of an artificial reef comes partly from the spaces created around and between its structures. A flat sandy bottom offers relatively little vertical relief. Bundled structures create edges, gaps and surfaces where animals can shelter, feed or attach themselves.The Yarmouth site has been associated with a range of marine life, including black sea bass, scup, tautog, summer flounder, winter flounder and lobsters. Other species recorded on the reef include blue mussels, cunner, butterfish, longfin squid and knobbed whelk.The reef therefore became more than a collection of objects placed underwater. Over time, marine organisms colonised the available surfaces, while fish used the added structure as part of the surrounding habitat. Massachusetts' artificial reef planning documents describe earlier monitoring at Yarmouth as showing stabilisation of the structures, colonisation by marine organisms and increased recreational fishing activity.The original 1978 deployment was not the end of the project. In 2014, the town and the Division of Marine Fisheries received permits to add further reef material in parts of the site where surveys had identified lower concentrations of existing structures.More material was added again around 2019 and early 2020. This included retired concrete buoy sinkers from the US Coast Guard, granite blocks recovered from demolition projects and other concrete material. More than 3,000 cubic yards of new material were involved across the two deployment efforts.The later additions also changed the character of the reef. Rather than relying only on the original tyre bundles, the site began incorporating approved construction and infrastructure materials that could provide similar physical relief. A Massachusetts habitat-enhancement project, for example, used more than 2,200 cubic yards of material to create additional structured habitat within an undeveloped part of the permitted reef area.

Some shells were used directly, while others were heated at around 900°C to make quicklime before being combined with crushed shell. The mixture was moulded and left to harden, producing tiles that became part of the building's exterior. By using discarded bedding and oyster shells, the project tested whether everyday waste could serve a useful purpose while reducing the demand for conventional building materials.The University of Brighton team developed the tiles as part of a project exploring how waste materials could be reused in construction. The mixture was then pressed into silicone moulds and left for several days. After adding water, the mixture underwent a natural chemical reaction that made it hard. Article Title: This Hawaii company is making boats from volcanic rock and recycled plastic instead of traditional materials
Article Text:
3D printed RHIB hull. Image Credit: Voltage Vessels

Company in Hawaii making boats from volcanic rock and recycled plastic

The company aims to print replacement hulls closer to operational areas. Image Credit: Voltage Vessels

Eclipse X9 is built for large-scale printing

Eclipse X9 is designed to work across different types of equipment. Image Credit: Defense Blog

What makes the material suitable for use in the ocean

A six-metre printed boat hull has already entered evaluation

The idea is to move production closer to where boats are needed

Recycling is another part of the company's plan

A Hawaii-based company is taking a unique approach to boat manufacturing by combining recycled plastic with volcanic rock-derived basalt fibre. Voltage Vessels, a startup based in Hawaii, has developed a material called ‘Eclipse X9’ which can be used in large-scale 3D printing and is being tested for marine applications. The material has already become part of the company's plans for printed boats, including a 6-metre hull submitted for US maritime defence evaluation. By replacing some conventional manufacturing processes with digital designs and printable composites, the company is exploring whether boats and marine structures could eventually be produced closer to where they are needed, instead of manufacturing them far away and then transporting them over long distances.Traditional boatbuilding can require specialised molds, extensive labour and fixed manufacturing facilities. Voltage Vessels is exploring a different route, centred on 3D printing and a composite material called Eclipse X9.According to Defence Blog, the Hawaii-based company was founded and is led by Sam Young. Its Eclipse X9 material combines recycled PETG plastic with chopped basalt fibre, creating a structural composite designed specifically for marine and defence applications.Basalt is a volcanic rock, making it a particularly notable ingredient for a company based in Hawaii, where volcanic activity has shaped the islands. The company processes basalt fibre and recycled plastic into a material that can be used as feedstock for 3D printers.Instead of relying entirely on conventional boatbuilding methods, the approach allows a digital design to be transformed into a physical structure through additive manufacturing, or 3D printing.According to 3D Printing Industry, Voltage Vessels has released Eclipse X9 for large-format additive manufacturing after several years of development. The material is now commercially available as both pellets and filament and is being evaluated at several facilities using different printing platforms.The company is targeting a wide range of uses, including marine structures, buoys, unmanned surface vehicles, infrastructure components and other structures exposed to difficult coastal conditions.Eclipse X9 is designed to work across different types of equipment rather than being tied to one specific printer. The pellet version can be used in large industrial systems, while the filament is available for machines ranging from smaller desktop printers to larger printing units.This flexibility is important to the company’s wider manufacturing idea. Instead of building every marine structure at one central factory, the material could potentially support production at facilities closer to where a finished product is required.A boat material must be able to cope with long-term exposure to water, particularly saltwater. This is one of the main areas where Eclipse X9 has undergone testing. According to 3D Printing Industry, independent validation was carried out by the Advanced Structures and Composites Center at the University of Maine. The testing included mechanical assessments and analysis of the material for marine applications.In saltwater immersion trials lasting between 24-26 months, the composite retained more than 90% of its strength. The published performance figures also included tensile strength of 108.2 megapascals, bending strength of 112.98 megapascals and water absorption below 0.4 per cent.Its ability to retain strength while absorbing relatively little water is particularly important because prolonged water exposure can weaken materials used in boat hulls and other marine structures.The basalt fibre also adds properties that could make the composite suitable for specialised applications. 3D Printing Industry noted that basalt fibre is non-conductive and transparent to radio frequencies.The company’s technology is not limited to material testing. According to Defence Blog, the company has submitted a 6-metre rigid-hull inflatable boat (RHIB) for US maritime defence evaluation.RHIBs are fast boats which are commonly used for a variety of maritime operations. Traditionally, such boats can be made using materials including fibreglass or aluminium and often require specialised production facilities and tooling.The hull submitted by Voltage Vessels was printed using a large-format additive manufacturing system. The wider aim is to explore whether printed marine structures could support autonomous naval programmes and other maritime requirements.The company's broader proposal focuses on distributed manufacturing. Instead of producing boats only at a distant central facility and then shipping them to their final destination, digital designs could potentially be sent to regional manufacturing sites.Defence Blog reported that the company is thinking of Hawaii serving as an initial node in a framework intended to expand across the Indo-Pacific.Under this concept, regional facilities could use the same digital design files to produce hulls and other structural components. The process would reduce dependence on conventional molds and some of the supply chains involved in traditional boat manufacturing.This could be especially relevant in regions where transporting replacement vessels over long distances is difficult. Sending replacement hulls from the continental United States to locations across the Indo-Pacific can take considerable time and depend on available cargo transport.The company's concept is that locally available printing equipment and material could shorten that process by allowing structures to be manufactured nearer to their point of use.The use of recycled PETG is central to Eclipse X9. According to 3D Printing Industry, the composite supports closed-loop mechanical recycling, meaning finished parts can potentially be shredded, converted back into pellets and printed again.This approach could reduce the need to simply discard used printed structures. It could also have practical value in locations where waste disposal and the delivery of new materials are both challenging.The company sees possible applications beyond boats, including ocean-monitoring equipment, coastal structures, tooling and marine infrastructure. By combining basalt fibre with recycled PETG and using large-scale 3D printing, the Hawaii company is testing whether boats of the future could be manufactured with different materials, recycled after use and produced much closer to where they are needed.
Article Summary: Company in Hawaii making boats from volcanic rock and recycled plastic. The company aims to print replacement hulls closer to operational areas. By replacing some conventional manufacturing processes with digital designs and printable composites, the company is exploring whether boats and marine structures could eventually be produced closer to where they are needed.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: With iPhone Duo, Apple makes entry into foldable market
Article Text:
Apple's first foldable phone

NEW DELHI: Apple on Wednesday entered the foldable smartphone market with iPhone Duo, priced at Rs 2,99,900, taking on Samsung, Google and Chinese brands in a category it had stayed away from even as rivals spent years refining the form factor.The book-style device has a 5.5-inch outer screen and unfolds into a 7.8-inch display, effectively turning the phone into a small tablet.
