Article Title: Dire straits: Brand on the run as Trump suggests Hormuz can be renamed in his honor
Article Text:
Trump’s latest push to rename the Strait of Hormuz adds another chapter to his growing campaign of political branding and geographic renaming

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Donald Trump has rescued a canal, invaded a country, conquered a gulf, annexed a lake -- at least on American maps -- and put his name on a performing-arts center. He now appears to have set his sights on the hottest waterway on the planet.The MAGA boss suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” -- because if you cannot solve a problem, you can at least rename it.The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal purposes. Last week he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, saying the US had been treated badly by Canada. He then helpfully suggested that the Atlantic or Pacific could be next, saying, “We have a gulf and we have a lake…Now all we need is an ocean. ”The President, someone jibed, appears to be collecting bodies of water like refrigerator magnets.The joke became even better when Google Maps and Apple Maps fell in line.Google changed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users over the weekend. Apple followed on Tuesday. Canadians, however, continue to see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere may see both names. In other words, the lake has acquired the geographic equivalent of dual citizenship.The tech companies' compliance prompted criticism from illuminati who argue that private corporations should not allow political pressure to dictate historical and geographic nomenclature. MapQuest, an internet relic many Americans had forgotten existed, refused to make the change and suddenly discovered the most effective marketing strategy in Silicon Valley: stand up to Trump. Its downloads reportedly surged, giving it the kind reception normally reserved for rock bands that haven’t toured for a long time or sports legends making a comeback.There is also an awkward business joke buried underneath all this. Trump built his political persona partly on branding himself as a master businessman, but his corporate record includes repeated failures and bankruptcies in hotels and casinos; His casino empire alone went through multiple Chapter 11 restructurings. Trump-branded ventures have also included products and licensing deals that did not last.Late-night television has naturally treated Trump's naming obsession as premium material. The Atlantic, meanwhile, took the joke to its logical conclusion in a satirical vision of a future America in which everything is renamed “America” or “Trump,” leaving citizens unable to distinguish between brands of products, goods, and structures.Political analysts however see a serious calculation behind what many consider trolling. The renaming campaign sure is presidential theater -- cheap to stage, impossible for the internet and tv to resist, and almost guaranteed to ignite social media. But it also serves to distract people from more pressing issues -- such as cost of living and democracy going down the tubes.
Article Summary: Trump suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf Of America for US federal purposes.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: “Greatness comes from character, and character isn't formed…” - the lesson behind his powerful words
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jensen Huang

“Greatness comes from character, and character isn't formed out of smart people — it's formed out of people who have suffered.”

Understanding the meaning behind the quote

Why Huang puts so much weight on hardship

What the quote says about resilience

Lessons from Jensen Huang's words

Intelligence has limits: Understanding a problem quickly does not always mean having the resilience to stay with it longest.

Expectations must allow for reality: High expectations can exist alongside low resilience. When results fall short, the ability to adapt matters.

Failure can provide useful information: A mistake does not define someone's ability. It can show what needs to change when examined honestly.

Patience matters: Important technological developments can take years to reveal their full impact. Nvidia's early focus on graphics eventually connected with much broader computing needs.

Success is often measured in visible things: a degree, a promotion, a company that survives, or an invention that changes an industry. Jensen Huang has spent much of his career around those measures. As the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, he helped take a graphics-chip company founded in 1993 into one of the most important technology companies in the world. Yet when Huang was asked about what helps people become successful, he did not point first to intelligence or academic achievement. He spoke about hardship, resilience and the way difficult experiences can shape a person. His view is summed up in a line that puts character ahead of raw ability.Huang made the remark while speaking to students at Stanford University in 2024.The distinction Huang makes is between being capable and being able to withstand difficult circumstances. Intelligence can help someone understand a complicated problem. Education can provide knowledge.Technical skill can make it possible to build something that others cannot. None of those qualities, by themselves, guarantee that a person will keep going when a plan fails or when a long period of uncertainty arrives. It is reflected in how someone behaves when circumstances become uncomfortable. A person may have to accept criticism, recover from a mistake, work through disappointment or continue making decisions without knowing whether the outcome will be favourable.Huang's argument is not that suffering automatically produces a good character. Difficult experiences can affect people in many different ways. His point is that hardship can provide situations in which resilience, patience and judgement have to be developed rather than simply understood in theory.Huang has often spoken about the difficult parts of building a company. Nvidia was founded in 1993 by Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, initially with a focus on computer graphics. The company later developed the GPU, with the GeForce 256 introduced in 1999 as a landmark in the development of programmable computer graphics. Its technology eventually became central to parallel computing and artificial intelligence.That path was not simply a straight rise. Huang has described Nvidia's history as containing serious mistakes and periods when the company's future was uncertain. He has discussed several early challenges and what he described as near-death experiences for the company.This helps explain why he speaks about suffering in such practical terms. For someone who has spent decades running a technology company through changing markets, setbacks are not unusual events. They are part of the work.Resilience is easy to discuss when nothing is going wrong. It becomes more complicated when a person has invested years in something and still does not know whether it will work.Huang's comments suggest that resilience is partly built through exposure to those situations. A setback forces a person to make another decision. Failure can require an adjustment rather than an immediate answer. Repeated difficulties can also change how someone views risk, expectations and responsibility.That does not mean people should seek suffering for its own sake. Huang's comments are better understood as an observation about unavoidable hardship. Difficult experiences happen in education, careers, businesses and ordinary personal life. His argument is that avoiding every uncomfortable experience may also mean avoiding some of the situations in which resilience develops.
Article Summary: Huang made the remark while speaking to students at Stanford University in 2024. The distinction Huang makes is between being capable and being able to withstand difficult circumstances. Huang's argument is not that suffering automatically produces a good character. Difficult experiences happen in education, careers, businesses and ordinary personal life.
